hook: In April 2023, war broke out in Sudan. Within a year, millions had fled their homes (UNHCR, 2024). Some crossed into Chad and Egypt; most stayed inside Sudan, in camps and with relatives. Far away, a Filipino nurse boards a plane to take a job in Canada. All are migrants. What separates them?

prereq.q: Drought ruins a family’s crops at home. What is the drought?
prereq.why: Problems at the origin push people out.

prereq.q: Which of Ravenstein’s laws says many people move from village to town to city?
options: Long-distance migrants go to big cities
prereq.why: Ravenstein found many migrants move in stages.

figure.caption: Forced and voluntary migration and their main types.

chain.cause: Forced migrants stay inside their country
Forced migrants cross a border and ask for protection
chain.effect: they are asylum seekers until a decision, and refugees if protection is granted

chain.cause: People choose to move for work, family or study
chain.effect: voluntary migration, often in steps or along chains of relatives

ideas: Forced migration: people are made to move (enslavement, war, persecution, disaster). Voluntary migration: people choose to move.
Forced types: refugee (crossed a border, granted protection), asylum seeker (asked, waiting), internally displaced person (stayed in the country).
Voluntary types: internal (interregional or intraregional), rural-to-urban, step, chain, guest worker, transnational and transhumance.
Real moves often mix choice and force, so explain the case instead of only naming a type.

misconception.wrong: Anyone who flees danger is a refugee.
misconception.right: A refugee has crossed an international border and been recognized as needing protection. People who flee but stay in their own country are internally displaced persons; people who have asked for protection and are waiting are asylum seekers.

summary: Forced migrants are made to move, as refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons or, in the past, enslaved people. Voluntary migrants choose to move, within a country (internal, rural-to-urban) or abroad, in steps or along chains of relatives, as guest workers, as transnational migrants who keep ties to two countries, or seasonally with herds (transhumance).
